doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Ancestor Samuel Sewall and the Thoreau romance
summary: Collier describes his ancestor the hanging judge Samuel Sewall and his great-grandmother's thwarted romance with Thoreau.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Is there? Well it’s interesting. Yeah, one of the hanging judges, Samuel Sewall of the Bay Colony was one of my ancestors and he’s famous for being the hanging judge of course. But the important thing, one of the important things about him in addition to that was that he wrote the first anti-slavery tract produced in the United States. He wrote, his principle was I just do not see how God is differentiating between blacks and whites, they were all human and therefore slavery should not exist. That was his position on this, and that’s been forgotten about him in all the calumny that’s been heaped on him for the hanging judge business. But in the family we are very pleased about that because if he hadn’t been a hanging judge Arthur Miller never would have been able to write The Crucible. So you see we’re responsible for some great books. Just to follow that line of thought, we were responsible for some other rather important books. My great grandmother, through various family connections, knew the family of Henry David Thoreau. And in fact my great great grandmother boarded with the Thoreaus. And Thoreau fell in love with my great grandmother and wanted to marry her and there was a whole business about that and the family, my family, wouldn’t hear of it because the Thoreaus really, they didn’t have any money, they were kind of — couldn’t quite get their stuff together.
